# Industry evolution in steel

#### As part of the Institute's 150th anniversary, our Iron and Steel Group looked at 150 years of the iron & steel industry, with commentary about the past, the present, and potential future opportunities.

© Ant Rozetsky/Unsplash

Over the last 150 years, hundreds of engineers, scientists and technicians have cut their teeth taking society forward via developments in the Iron and Steel arena.

This section is a tour around the manufacturing processes over the period.

1869 - 1900: The Bessemer Years - The Bessemer Process
Prior to the Bessemer process developed in 1856, wrought iron was the material of choice for infrastructure, and  shipbuilding. The benefits of steel were well known from the manufacture of cutlery  small engineering components and armour, due to its improved properties, particularly ductility  and ease of shaping, however the existing process was long and  laborious and products could only be made in small batches. Bessemer's invention of injection of hot air blasted through liquid Iron to decarburise the iron, meant that steel for the first time could be manufactured in large quantities, at a fraction of the cost and time of the cementitious process. Suddenly steel was available to all enabling the growth of rail transport systems and shipbuilding. While the process was patented in 1860 and the first cast made on the 18th June 1859 it would be another 20 years before the process was widely accepted.

 

The initial slow implementation of the Bessemer process was due to the high volatility of production (oxygen) and the presense of high phosphorous in the ores. Initially for high quality steels the Bessemer process relied on the procurement of low phosphorus ores from Sweden and South Wales, which limited the production. This was coupled with the slow acceptance for shipbuilding where it wasn’t until a report by Lloyds register in 1869 that steel was certified for use in Shipbuilding. The Lloyds register of ships in 1889 still shows the transition from Iron and wood to Steel ships, though increasingly the introduction of large steam powered ships, would  accelerate the transition to steel. By 1900 the UK made 61% of the worlds ships. This had also transformed the industrial map of Britain with the traditional wood based southern yards giving way to the mainly Northern based yards of the 1880s onwards, due to the abundance of ironmaking, and coal resources. By the end of the century steel had also come to displace wrought iron in structural steel, with the building of the Forth Bridge (1890 54KT) and Blackpool Tower (1894 2.5KT).

Despite the enormous step change the Bessemer process brought, some significant developments were needed to enable bulk production.The deoxidation of the steel relied on the invention of Robert Foster Mushet, who in collaboration with the EBBW Vale Company  patented the process of the addition of ‘a triple compound of  iron, manganese and carbon to deoxidise the bath before teeming the metal into the mould’. Unfortunateley this wasn’t taken up initially and the patent expired in 1859. When commercial production began in the Bessemer Works, Mushet received no royalties, though Bessemer voluntarily paid him a pension for the rest of his life.

The problem of using high phosphorus ores and dephosphorising was finally solved after a series of experiments by various researchers particularly Snelus ( lime based brick lining) and Sydney Gilchrist Thomas, in collaboration with Percy Carlisle Gilchrist, a chemist at Blaenavon Works. Although the lining isssues  had been solved the steelmaking performance proved erratic. J.E. Stead, also working at the Blaenavon works, experimented with blowing of lime through the tuyeres. He noted the effective removal of phosphorous during the overblow, reasoning that both basic and strongly oxidising conditions were required for effective removal of phosphorus. The findings of all this work were presented by Sidney Gilchrist Thomas  on his seminal paper 'basic steelmaking' at the spring meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute in 1879.

The Bessemer process would remain in operation until 1978 (in the production of forging ingots for which it was well suited), though it was progressively phased out for bulk steelmaking in the period 1900-1920 with the advent of open hearth steelmaking and the introduction of Electric Arc steelmaking.

All steel was cast into ingots or moulds for subsequent forging or rolling into semi products. Forging was carried out by the steam hammer and rolling by the stream driven two-high mills of the time. Much of the forging and rolling processes had been around from antiquity, but enhanced from the dramatic increase in force from steam drives.

Research and development during early industrialisation
Although steel had been researched since the early 1800s the methodology was largely empirical and based on the observed properties, from the use of small test samples. The main driver for research following Bessemer's invention, and the step up in scale was to control the chemistry of the reaction, particularly deoxidising (using Manganese) and dephosphorising using lime, in both Bessemer converters and open hearth. Each steelworks generally had resident chemists, whos main focus was to control the process, and increase productivity.

The technique of using spectroscopy to  analyse the metal, had been experimented with in the mid 1800s and was now employed to apply science to process control. The extract opposite is from Bessemer heats in Sheffield, showing the  correlation between the observation by eye and the spectroscopic analysis. This gave rise to controlling the C and P and minimising overblow.

Metallography was in its infancy, but developed rapidly from the 1880s largely as a result of work of a Sheffield geologist Henry Clifton Sorby, with a seminal paper relating changes in microstructure to changes in composition and processing, presented at a meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute in 1884. He named the pearly structure sorbite, but it would later be changed to pearlite, due to its ‘pearly‘ nature under optical microscopy.

Temperature measurement was crude until the platinum–rhodium thermocouple introduced in the latter stages of the century. This allowed for experimentation on actual temperature changes and combined with the metallography of the day would lead to the first edition of the Iron- Iron carbide equilibrium diagram  in 1899, which is still researched to this day.

1900-1960: The growth of open hearth and electric arc - early 20th Century process evolution
Shortly after the Bessemer process in 1856, Sir William Siemens invented the open hearth process in 1867, by merging two technologies of regenerative heating with Martins process of diluting pig iron with wrought iron scrap prior to refining. The process, used preheating of the incoming air, combined with heating from regenerative waste gases, enabling much higher temperatures to be achieved. One key advantage over the Bessemer process was the ability to utilise scrap steel and wrought iron, which was abundant and cheap. The process also had a higher flexibility of raw material inputs, and closer control of the process, This led to a massive increase in applications for open hearth steel, and its rapid rise in the last decade of the 19th Century would see it become the dominant steelmaking process until its decline in the 1960s. At the start of the century the acid open hearth process was the dominant process, however the iron ore demand could not be satisfied by sourcing of relatively scare low phosphorous ores, and so the basic process rapidly became the dominant process by 1920 onwards.

The carbon arc was discovered by Sir Humphrey Davy in 1810, and small arc furnaces were patented by Siemens in 1878, however enhancement to bulk steel commercialisation awaited  introduction of large scale electrical power and the  production  of robust carbon electrodes. The first commercial batch of electric arc steel was manufactured in France from the  Heroult process in 1900. The EAF has seen steady growth over the 20th Century largely related to higher power densities and efficiencies, and its main advantage of relatively  installation cost compared to Integrated works. From the early days Electric Arc has always been the favoured route for the production of alloy steels, due to its ability to melt metals from scrap or ingots. This differentiation  exists to the day with the bulk  ‘low alloy’ steels generally made via BOS Integrated plants and  alloy steels such as stainless, and tungsten tool steels made via EAF.

 In the first half of the 20th Century, the driver in alloys steels was to develop armour steels for gun barrels and  armour plating. Experiments in the 19th Century had shown chrome and nickel improving hardness and toughness, but the process was difficult to control, until the advantages of low carbon were later understood. It was while experimenting with armour  plate steels that one Harry Brearley ‘discovered’ the corrosion effects, and produced the first stainless steel in 1913.

Early 20th century technological developments in steel
The main hot working processes of  rolling, forging tube making and wire drawing had been established practise in the 19th Century. In the first half of the 20th Century these would be significantly enhanced, with the development of the electric motor, increasing  the power, and  introducing process control. The electric motor also paved the way for continuous mills, initially for bar and rod but then quickly for the production of strip around 1920.

Up until the 1920s  the main joining method for steel had been riveting which was time consuming and wasteful due to the material overlap needed. Gas welding had been invented in the late 19th century, and though adopted for some tube applications, was not widely used. The driver for adoption of the technology was the time leading up to and during WW1, where productivity was key in supporting the war effort with tanks, aircraft and ships. Although this was a great success, there were problems emphasised by the Liberty ships where some broke in half due to brittle fracture. This however spurned the new  science area of fatigue and fracture, leading to the drive for low sulphur, low phosphorous steels, and the  the derivation of the Carbon equivalent formula to avoid preheating, which drove carnon levels down.

The Iron and Steel Institute formed in 1869 had fostered collaboration between the steel companies, however up until the 1930s the main research was carried out in works laboratories. The 1930s heralded the introduction of ‘big science’, and the steel industry saw opportunities to  benefit from large scale research, graduating from the existing committees of the Iron and Steel Industrial Research Council (formed in 1929), to the British Iron and Steel  Research Association formed in 1944. The group also undertook foreign sponsored projects  through associations with such bodies as the International Flame Research Foundation in he Netherlands and Belgium, now superceded by RFCS. The laboratories included Battersea in London, Sketty Hall in South Wales, Imperial College London (fundamental Ironmaking) , Normanby in Middlesborough, and Hoyle Street in Sheffield. Later the laboratories of United Steels in Rotherham ( STC), a new centre in Grangetown (now MPI) and Scottish labs in  Motherwell would be added to the mix. Some of the pioneering work in these labs, paved the way to the step change in productivity and quality that occurred from the 1960s.
